quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /t/ ending "not" to the bilabial sound that opens "married". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /t/ becomes /p/ in "not married" to match the bilabial consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /d/ at the end of "recommend". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "doctor"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /d/ at the end of "recommend" disappears before the consonant that starts "doctor".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "hot" to "meals". Is it still /t/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /t/ meets a bilabial sound, the /t/ shifts to /p/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "hot meals".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "expand business" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /d/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "expand business", the /d/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /d/ ending "bread" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the bilabial sound in "basket"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /d/ moves to a bilabial position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /b/ in "bread basket".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "loud". With a bilabial consonant starting "music" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /d/ ending "loud" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /d/ becomes /b/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "music".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /t/ where "contest" meets "winner" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /t/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "contest winner" aloud and you'll notice the /t/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "ten clients" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /n/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /n/ rarely stays /n/ before a velar sound — it assimilates to /ŋ/, which is exactly what you hear in "ten clients".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "trust" get pronounced before "me", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "trust" is the one that goes missing before "me".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Picture how a native speaker would say "packed lunch" in a fast, everyday sentence. Is every single consonant still there?
quests.explanation: This is a textbook case of consonant-cluster elision: the /t/ between two consonants is dropped to keep speech fluent and effortless in "packed lunch".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The tongue is already anticipating "bag"'s bilabial sound before it even finishes "right". What happens to /t/ as a result?
quests.explanation: The change from /t/ to /p/ at the end of "right" happens because the following bilabial consonant in "bag" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "world" is trapped between two other consonants right before "tour". What usually happens to a stop consonant stuck in that position?
quests.explanation: Rather than pronounce all three consonants back to back, speakers cut the /d/ from "world" entirely. The result flows straight from the first consonant into "tour".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "seven" and "months" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /n/ ending "seven" adopts the bilabial quality of the sound in "months", surfacing as /m/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This isn't a case of a sound vanishing from "ten" — it's still there, just different. What does /n/ turn into before the velar sound in "guests"?
quests.explanation: Notice that the /n/ ending "ten" isn't deleted the way it would be in elision — it survives, just transformed into /ŋ/ to match the velar sound beginning "guests".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ at the end of "must" is about to meet a bilabial sound in "pay". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a bilabial consonant, /t/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "must pay", /t/ becomes /p/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "good meal" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /d/ stay a /d/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /d/ ending "good" turns into /b/ because "meal" begins with a bilabial consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A velar consonant is coming up in "coffee". What does that do to the /t/ just before it in "hot"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /t/ anticipate the velar sound ahead. So in "hot coffee", /t/ is pronounced as /k/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen closely at the boundary of "cold" and "call" — count the consonants stacking up. Does the /d/ still make it into the sentence?
quests.explanation: In fast, connected speech, a /d/ wedged between consonants almost always disappears. That's what you'll hear in "cold call" — the /d/ goes silent.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /t/ ending "light" to the velar sound that opens "coat". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /t/ becomes /k/ in "light coat" to match the velar consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "quiet" to "mood". Is it still /t/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?

quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "hit" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the bilabial sound in "pause"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a bilabial position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /p/ in "hit pause".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "old news" naturally, without pausing between the words. Is the /d/ audible, or does it disappear into the next consonant?
quests.explanation: Elision removes a sound completely rather than merely blending it. Here the /d/ vanishes from "old" so the phrase moves directly into "news".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This pair, "correct list", creates a tricky consonant sequence. Which sound do fluent speakers simplify away — and is it really gone, or just quieter?
quests.explanation: Speakers naturally avoid three consonants in a row, so the /t/ is dropped rather than forced through. That's why "correct list" sounds smoother without it.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Fluent speech avoids awkward consonant pile-ups. Where exactly does that simplification happen in "next level"?
quests.explanation: This cluster is simplified by deleting the /t/ altogether — not weakening it, not shifting it, just leaving it out — which is the defining feature of elision in "next level".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "quite". With a bilabial consonant starting "busy" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /t/ ending "quite" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /t/ becomes /p/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "busy".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "count" alone, then "down" alone — both consonants are clear. Now blend them at speed. What happens to the /t/ in between?
quests.explanation: Notice that nothing replaces the /t/ — it isn't weakened or swapped for another sound, it's simply omitted. That full deletion is what separates elision from assimilation in "count down".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A stop consonant squeezed between two other consonants rarely survives in fast speech. Listen for the /t/ in "post code" — is it there?
quests.explanation: Consonant clusters like this one are common at word boundaries in English, and the middle stop is almost always the casualty. The /t/ drops out of "post code" for exactly that reason.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "waste money" quickly. The consonants pile up right around the /t/ in "waste" — does it survive the crowd, or get squeezed out?
quests.explanation: When /t/ sits between two other consonants, English speakers routinely drop it to keep the rhythm smooth. In "waste money", the /t/ disappears rather than being pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "green bag" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /n/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /n/ rarely stays /n/ before a bilabial sound — it assimilates to /m/, which is exactly what you hear in "green bag".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant cluster forming between "shift" and "schedule". In natural speech, one sound in that cluster usually disappears. Which one?
quests.explanation: Three consonants in a row are hard to articulate cleanly, so speakers simplify by deleting the middle one. That's exactly what happens to the /t/ in "shift schedule" — it's dropped, not just softened.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.
